newsitem.title: USA: CBOT panel says USDA acreage data not set in stone.
newsitem.headline: CBOT panel says USDA acreage data not set in stone.

text.p: Calls fluctuated for the direction of Chicago Board of Trade grain and soy complex futures prices as a CBOT panel Monday cautioned that USDA's acreage data in its March 31 planting intentions report is not "set in stone."
"Farmers can change acreage and they will do so depending on weather," said Terry Francl, senior economist for the American Farm Bureau Federation.
Traders expected volatile dealings, saying November soybeans would open 10 to 20 cents per bushel lower.
Early calls were mixed for nearby corn contracts and new crop corn was seen four to five cents lower.
The U.S. Agriculture Department on Monday said U.S. farmers this year would plant 68.8 million acres of soybeans, well above trade expectations for 65.85 million.
Corn acreage was expected to total 81.416 million, above average analysts' expectations for 80.92 million.

Traders and analysts said the CBOT markets could be a mixed bag in early dealings Monday with the nearby contracts supported by the government's quarterly stocks report and the new crop months pressured by the bearish acreage estimate.

USDA Monday said the supply of corn in the U.S. as of March 1 totaled 4.494 billion bushels, below an average of analysts' expectations for 4.565 billion. The soybean stocks tally was at 1.078 billion bushels, below expectations for 1.093 billion bushels.
"We've been looking at phenomenal export sales and a great crush," said Andy Daniels, executive vice president of LFG, referring to the lower-than-expected total for USDA's quarterly soybean stocks.
"Corn stocks suggest the feeding rates are higher than expected," Francl said. "Near-term corn prices should remain fairly firm."

USDA's outlook for spring wheat seedings at 17.8 million acres was a result of high corn and soybean prices and was also linked to heavy snowcover in portions of the U.S. Northern Plains which could lead to delayed planting in that key U.S. spring wheat growing region.
"Many expect even more reductions," Daniels said.
Daniels and Francl said farmers in the U.S. Northern Plains spring wheat area would seed as many acres as possible to soybeans and corn at the expense of wheat because of the high prices.
"We have a situation in beans that's not all that different from corn a year ago," Francl said. U.S. corn prices shot to record levels roughly a year ago due to tight supplies of corn.
"Whether or not the current price of beans is high enough to slow demand remains to be seen," Francl said.
